item.content:encoded:
When Billy Crystal lost his home of 46 years to the Palisades fires—the house where he raised his children, watched his grandchildren grow up and shared a life with his wife, Janice Crystal—he said, "Every inch of our house was filled with love. Beautiful memories that can't be taken away." Crystal's new one-man show, 860, is named for that address and revisits those memories. Through his signature blend of humor and heart, Crystal weaves an intimate narrative that explores loss, resilience and the power of community.
For director Scott Ellis, helping Crystal bring his deeply personal story to the Broadway stage meant uncovering the universal themes within it. The Tony nominee spoke to Broadway.com about workshopping the show, early audience reactions and what he discovered along the way.
When did Billy approach you about 860?
About a year ago. He was meeting with directors and I was one of them. I got a call and I said, "Sure, it's Billy Crystal. Yes." So I met him and as he tells the story, he thought we'd be there for 20, 30 minutes. We ended up being there for two hours just talking, and him telling his story and showing me photos. I was doing Art at the time, and he came to see it and then we had more conversations and he asked me to do it.
So it's been a work in progress for a while.
We started sitting at a table reading, and then the next step was the changes. It's changed quite a lot. We went into another table read where I invited 20 people in. And then we ended up doing it live in front of an audience for two nights. We took a break, came back and did it for another five nights in front of audiences. It was sort of like a tiny out-of-town tryout for us, just to start hearing it in front of people and learning what we needed to learn.
Because it's just the two of you, did you workshop more than you normally would as a director?
I guess so. He had the story. He had this incredible beginning and ending, which I walked away [from] going, "This is perfect." Then it was just what you're doing in the middle, telling more stories. It was a great journey with him. I think most important was getting it in front of people so we could hear how people were reacting and what needed to be cut, things that worked, things that didn't work.
What made you want to get involved?
What I felt. The fact that he's ultimately talking about loss—I mean, listen, he lost everything. Their family lost everything. So I thought, how do we relate to that? I've never had that experience. But when you really delve into it, what he's talking about is loss, is the next chapter. If this had happened when he was 25, it would be a very different experience, but it happened much later in life. What are the next chapters? What are those decisions? What does stuff mean to you? I kept finding things that I thought were universal, larger questions that people who didn't go through what he and Janice went through would still be able to connect with.
Like 860, Billy's first one-man show, 700 Sundays, tackled loss. Did you discuss that work?
We didn't talk too much about it. He obviously did it and knows it well, but I wanted to focus on how we were planning to tell this story. It was very different than 700 Sundays. It's a very successful, wonderful piece of theater, so you can't pretend it didn't happen. But the focus was this story.
Why do you think Billy is so adept at telling stories of tragedy through comedy?
Well, first of all, that's who he is. He talks about how important laughter is in his life. There is the framework of something horrible that happened, but he goes back into memories of stuff that was lost and that triggers some incredibly funny stories. He's a remarkable storyteller and certainly knows comedy better than most. I think when people hear it's about the loss of his home, you think, "That's going to be a really sad evening." It's poignant. There is some sadness, but there's a great deal of joy also, of what he's discovering and him moving on. And I found that incredibly moving, that despite everything he was still saying, "We're moving on, and family is so important." His family and his wife, Janice, you see that tightness and you see that's how you can survive some of this.
How have audiences responded to Billy's storytelling?
It was our first preview, and I remember thinking, "Oh, they're connecting to this." They want to listen to this story. Visually, we've done a lot of different interesting things that I wanted to put into the storytelling. So I think that helps [make it] a theatrical experience. But it just boils down to one person who's telling a story. And I don't know if there's anyone better out there who can tell a story as well as he does. So the audience leaned in immediately, and they go on this journey from beginning to end.
"I kept finding things that I thought were universal, larger questions that people who didn't go through what he and Janice went through would still be able to connect with." —Scott Ellis
How did the visuals come together?
Billy has and had in his life a lot of photos and videos. When we first met, he showed me a chunk of them. He showed me the beginning of when the fire was coming, the discovery, and he showed me the end when he went back to see what was left. That was the framework, so in between, how do you tell the story? Well, through a lot of his photos. We have the incredible Hana Kim who's doing the projections and all the art, helping to tell that story visually. Billy would come in and say, "Oh, I have this photo," and we'd look at it, or, "I have this video." So it was just finding what was fitting in this puzzle. And then Marc Shaiman coming in and scoring it, I don't think any of us thought it would go as far as it has. But I love it and it makes it for, I think, a unique evening.
And the set is a recreation of his former home office?
We decided to bring the office in a little bit of an abstract way, meaning, it is his office, but visually it's all toned down because it's all memory. He's remembering the office. Everything he talks about, I wanted it to come from the office. And, as [scenic designer] Scott Pask said so beautifully, setting this in the office helped propel why we're telling these stories. He's such a brilliant designer. You could do it without anything, just some slides and projections, but I think we've all worked hard to make it a theatrical event.
This must be emotional for Billy as well. Why did he want to share his story this way?
I think he would have to answer this. But again, because he's a storyteller, I always ask him, "Did you think at all that one day you would tell this story?" And he said, "Yes." I thought, "That's so interesting." And again, that's who he is. But somewhere in all of this, in the back of his mind, he thought, "I'm going to tell this story," and I thought that was remarkable. It's really just a reminder of how you move forward after tragedy. I think you do it with friends and family if you're lucky to have them. I know that helped him get through this and get up to the stage.
What can audiences expect from 860?
I never say, "I hope the audience walks away with this," because everyone will have a different experience with it, you know? But I do think watching, being able to connect with someone who has gone through what he and his family went through, and that he did get on the other side of it—he's changed, all of us would be. But the fact that he's gotten on the other side and still being able to move forward, I find incredibly moving. He didn't give up where I think a lot of people could have given up and said, "I've lost it all." And so there's a celebration of life during what was the hardest thing he's ever gone through—he says that. And I think that's part of getting to know him. I think that is who he is. He keeps living, he keeps moving forward.
860 is now in previews, opening October 21 at the Imperial Theatre. Get tickets!

item.content:encoded:
After a discrepancy in comments involving Aaron Judge’s calf injury, Yankees manager Aaron Boone said Thursday that “we’re all in this together.”
Judge took issue Wednesday night with Boone characterizing the slugger’s calf strain as having a “moderate” grade.
“We’ve talked a little bit about it,” Boone said before Thursday night’s series finale against the Tampa Bay Rays in the Bronx.
“I don’t want to get too much into that, but at the end of the day, we’re all in this together, and in his case, trying to get him right and get him healthy so he can be an option for us here at some point. We’re also going to listen to the injury. I see it as just a passionate player that’s doing all he can to get back for his teammates.”
Judge landed on the 10-day injured list Saturday with a right calf strain, putting his playoff status in question.
While the Yankees have not disclosed the grade of the strain, Boone on Tuesday said it was “moderate.” Boone also said that day that he was “not expecting” Judge to be back for the Yankees’ Wild Card playoff series, which begins Tuesday, but didn’t rule anything out.
Judge, meanwhile, reiterated Wednesday night that he hopes to return in time for next week’s postseason opener.
“Everybody’s ‘moderate’ is a little different,” Judge said. “I think your moderate is a little different than my moderate, and so on and so on. So I don’t know why [Boone] used those words, but I’m trying to come back as soon as I can.”
Broadly, the Boston Sports Medicine & Research Institute considers a moderate calf strain to be of the second-degree and says that grade of injury typically requires three to six weeks of rest and recovery. Judge suffered the injury on Sept. 16.
The Yankees have not disclosed a timeline for Judge, who had returned on Sept. 8 after missing the previous 84 games due to a fractured rib.
“The bottom line is Aaron and I have always had an amazing relationship, and still do, and will,” Boone said. “This is about a player that is pouring everything he possibly can into being ready, and we’re gonna support that. When he’s ready, we’ll make a call of when that is, based on how he’s doing. It’s Thursday today. We may not make that call until Tuesday morning.”
Judge shared a similar sentiment Wednesday, calling Boone “my guy” and saying the manager “makes the right decisions.”
“My goal is to come back as soon as I can,” Judge said. “That’s what we’re doing right now. So if [Boone] says I’m not going to be ready, I got no control over that. I got control over what I can do to try to get back as soon as I can.”
Judge — a three-time American League MVP, including in 2024 and 2025 — is hitting .241 with 18 home runs, 41 RBI and an .871 OPS in 66 games this season.
The 34-year-old Judge received a Platelet-Poor Plasma (PPP) injection in his calf on Monday. Judge has not resumed hitting, Boone said Thursday.
“He’s doing all the things in the training room, all the modalities that he can take advantage of,” Boone said. “He’s moving on the treadmill, things like that, doing the different exercises to get that calf healed.”

item.content:encoded:
Lane Kiffin’s departure from Ole Miss has always been described as a breakup. One person leaves for someone else, and the other is left angry or depressed or both. The resentment builds fast, and there’s that instinct to get revenge.
In relationships, revenge can look like anything. New car. New clothes. Better job. New partner who makes the old one look like a mistake.
Then you run into each other and get to show you’re better off without them. That’s the moment.
Ole Miss got its moment Saturday night in front of 70,033 people at Vaught-Hemingway Stadium. The Rebels beat Kiffin and LSU’s $50 million roster, and it felt like bumping into an ex while wearing designer clothes, driving a Ferrari and sitting next to someone who’s clearly an upgrade.
What comes next, though, is usually just as hard as the breakup: moving on.
This column isn’t to say Ole Miss fans should forgive, forget or suddenly wish Kiffin well. It’s OK to hope LSU loses because, well, it’s LSU and that’s what Ole Miss fans do. But there is a difference between remembering something and continuing to live in it.
If fans keep bringing up Kiffin in every social media or message board post, they’re still allowing him to take up an enormous amount of space in Ole Miss football. If everything is framed through Kiffin, does the program ever truly become Pete Golding’s?
“Kiffin never did this,” or “This proves Ole Miss didn’t need Kiffin,” serve no purpose beyond momentary gratification.
Even positive comparisons have the same effect. Ole Miss making the playoffs becomes about Kiffin. Golding winning a big game becomes about Kiffin.
At some point, continuing to define Pete Golding’s Ole Miss program by its relationship to Lane Kiffin does Golding almost as much of a disservice as constantly comparing a new quarterback to the one he replaced.
It can also drown out what Ole Miss is accomplishing on the field.
This is a team with postseason aspirations. There are stars like Trinidad Chambliss, Kewan Lacy, Deuce Alexander, Will Echoles and Suntarine Perkins, along with a head coach who has quickly become one of the most popular figures around the program.
They deserve to be the center of attention more than the coach who chose to leave. Every conversation about what Kiffin tweeted or what LSU did Saturday is a conversation that isn’t about the Ole Miss team actually playing.
And you better believe the players and coaches see the talk. They’ll always say the right thing about not paying attention to that stuff, but they’re human, and there have been times when the conversation is impossible to ignore.
They’re also constantly asked about Kiffin, LSU, how this season compares to last season and how Golding differs from the coach he replaced.
Some of that is unavoidable. After beating then-No. 24 Louisville in the season opener, Chambliss was asked about LSU during a SportsCenter interview. That was two weeks before the Tigers would come to Oxford, and it was just another example of how often Ole Miss is viewed through the lens of LSU and Kiffin.
The more Kiffin remains part of the daily conversation around Ole Miss, the harder it becomes for the people inside the program to completely leave that chapter behind.
Again, this column isn’t about convincing anyone to hope Kiffin wins the rest of LSU’s games this season. The anger over his departure is justified. The 32-24 win over LSU last Saturday provided the outlet for that anger to be unleashed.
But staying obsessed with Kiffin keeps him at the center of Ole Miss football instead of Golding, Chambliss, Lacy and a team with realistic hopes of making the College Football Playoff.
There’s also a selfish reason for fans to move on: Ole Miss football is pretty fun right now.
This team is good. It has stars. It has legitimate postseason goals. If every big win is followed by wondering what Kiffin thinks, then part of the experience is still being defined by someone who left.
At some point, Ole Miss fans should be able to enjoy Ole Miss success simply because it belongs to Ole Miss.
Ultimately, fans are cheating themselves by experiencing the program’s current success primarily through their feelings about somebody who is no longer part of it.
Because the best revenge isn’t making Kiffin watch Ole Miss succeed.
It’s eventually not caring whether he’s watching.

Stars and fans debate changing attitudes towards the end of marriage
A candid discussion about divorce has turned into one of the latest celebrity debates in Pakistan, after veteran actor Saba Faisal questioned how society now responds to the end of marriages, prompting strong reactions from fellow actors and fans over grief, stigma and women's right to leave difficult relationships.
Faisal made the comments during an appearance on a TV's talk show, where she reflected on what she described as a significant change in social attitudes towards divorce.
"Before, when someone used to get divorced, there used to be a 'Sog' happening for months," Faisal said, referring to the mourning and grief that traditionally followed a divorce within a family. She contrasted that response with what she sees today, saying that divorced women could now casually mention their separation during conversations before moving on with their lives.
"Dads couldn't do anything, but now when we find out girls have got divorced, it's mentioned casually over a phone call," she said, adding that she had travelled abroad afterwards and tried to figure things out.
Her comments quickly spread online, with celebrities and social media users divided over whether the changing response to divorce represents a loss of sensitivity towards marriage or a greater willingness to acknowledge that marriages can end for different reasons.
Actor Hira Khan was among the strongest voices to respond. In an Instagram story, she wrote, "It's better to go through this than to be carried through a grave," before adding, "She needs help."
Khan argued that divorce should not be confused with celebration and highlighted the circumstances that can make leaving a marriage a matter of safety and dignity. "No one celebrates divorce," she wrote, adding that women have a religiously recognised right to seek it.
She also criticised what she described as the policing and shaming of women who choose to leave marriages. "I'm half your age, but I understand this much," Khan wrote. "Perhaps I was raised to understand that a woman's dignity, safety and right to choose matter."
Faisal's daughter, actor Sadia Faisal, subsequently appeared to respond to Khan, writing, "I wish I could see this so-called actress someday."
Actor Zoya Nasir also entered the discussion, writing in the comments, "Oh. My. God. I have SO much to say, with all due respect. What a dangerous and twisted narrative."
Not everyone, however, agreed with the criticism directed at Faisal. Dr Ejaz Waris offered a more conciliatory perspective, agreeing that divorce should not be celebrated while arguing that its emotional impact can extend to both families.
Fans similarly debated whether discussions about divorce had unfairly focused on the woman's family. Some pointed out that the husband's family can also experience grief, while others argued that the depth of that pain is difficult to understand until a divorce involves one's own daughter.
At the same time, some users defended Faisal, saying her central point was simply that divorce had become more normalised and that people could now return to their everyday lives more quickly following a separation.
The controversy comes shortly after Faisal spoke at length in another interview about the way her comments are handled online. She criticised the practice of editing remarks into short clips designed to generate viral reactions.
"The respect and honour we have built over our entire lives gets severely disturbed when a couple of words are spliced together and edited into the video," she said. Calling virality "a strange illness", Faisal said she had begun taking longer breaks from public appearances because of the way apparently ordinary remarks could be repackaged into controversy.
The actor has also previously attracted criticism for her views on marriage and family, making her latest comments part of a broader public discussion around traditional expectations and changing attitudes among younger generations.
At the heart of the latest debate is a distinction that has emerged repeatedly in the reactions: acknowledging divorce as a painful experience does not necessarily mean treating it as something desirable, while reducing stigma does not necessarily erase the grief associated with the end of a marriage.
For some of Faisal's critics, a woman being able to move forward after divorce is a sign of greater acceptance rather than indifference. For those defending her, the actor was drawing attention to what she sees as a decline in the social and familial gravity once attached to the breakdown of a marriage.

Lindsey Vonn debuted her new romance with fellow skier Matthieu Bailet on Wednesday in a social media post that sent her fans into a frenzy.
The Olympic alpine skier took to Instagram to share photos with her 30-year-old beau, who is a French alpine skier, and included several snaps of the pair vacationing together in a tropical location.
In one photo, the happy couple stood in the crystal-clear waters of a pool overlooking the sea and shared a sweet kiss, with Lindsey in a white bikini and Matthieu in light-colored swim shorts.
Another picture showcased the pair standing on a rock in the ocean as Matthieu held Lindsey from behind. The 41-year-old ended the carousel of photos with a snap of the pair cozying up together as they laid out over the water.
"About that time for a summer recap… pt 1," she wrote in the caption, as her friends and fans rushed to the comment section to exclaim over the new romance.
"Can't wait to see the summer recap part 2," Matthieu joked, alongside a kissing emoji, while Olympian Ilona Maher added: "The award for the hottest couple goes to…"
Tennis star Sloane Stephens chimed in: "HARD LAUNCH!!!!!!!" while another fan said: "Beautiful couple – wish you both all the best!"
Lindsey and Matthieu were first linked in May when they were seen spending time together in NYC. He competed in the Winter Olympic Games in China in 2022, and made his World Cup debut in 2016 in Switzerland.
Learn more about Lindsey below...
Moving on from Diego
Lindsey most recently dated businessman Diego Osorio from 2021 to 2025, and opened up about moving on after their heartbreaking split.
"Valentine's Day will look a little different for me this year...but I have my two dogs, so they'll be my Valentine's dates," she told People.
"I think with everything that's going on in my life, I sometimes have to keep reminding myself that it's a tough road, but I'm doing what I love to do, and I'm very lucky to be able to do it. But it doesn't mean that it's easy, and doesn't mean that it's not lonely at times."
Lindsey's dating history
Before Diego, the blonde beauty dated NHL star P.K. Subban from 2017 to 2020, former Los Angeles Rams coach Kenan Smith from 2016 to 2017, and Tiger Woods from 2013 to 2015.
The pro golfer announced their romance on Facebook in March 2013, writing: "Something nice that's happened off the course was meeting Lindsey Vonn. Lindsey and I have been friends for some time, but over the last few months we have become very close and are now dating."
"We thank you for your support and for respecting our privacy. We want to continue our relationship, privately as an ordinary couple and continue to compete as athletes."
Lindsey was married to pro skier Thomas Vonn from 2007 to 2011, and shared that their relationship taught her "a lot".
"I'm thankful for my years with Thomas," she told The New York Times. "So this is a difficult time. But I'm not worried that I can't be successful without him. I'm a strong and capable woman."

item.content:encoded:
- Editor’s Note: For the upcoming Sports Illustrated 2026–27 basketball preview magazine that will hit newsstands in October, SI spoke to anonymous scouts around the NBA about all 30 teams.
Portland punched above its weight in the Western Conference last season as the Trail Blazers earned the No. 7 seed with a 42–40 playoff record and a win over the Suns to open the play-in tournament. The Trail Blazers could fall out of the playoff mix this season, however.
Deni Avdija led the way last season in his breakout campaign, dropping 24.2 points per game and earning his first All-Star nod. He helped the Blazers have a say in the stacked conference following a sudden coaching change to start the year. Despite Tiago Splitter’s success as interim coach, Blazers owner Tom Dundon’s cost-cutting measures led to another coaching change over the offseason.
Longtime NBA assistant Micah Nori, who was most recently at the top of Chris Finch’s staff in Minnesota, is the new head man for the Blazers. Dundon didn’t want to put considerable funds into a head coach, which led to Splitter departing for the Bulls. Nori is a good hire, but he only has one guaranteed season on his three-year deal with team options on the final two seasons, which makes it difficult to build something sustainable on an already wonky roster.
“I don’t like how things look in Portland,” an anonymous NBA scout told Sports Illustrated. “Bad ownership, a coach with a bad contract and bad players together. Bad fits. Everything in Portland is a bad fit right now, top to bottom. They have got some guys. I like Toumani Camara. I like Shaedon Sharpe, when he is healthy. But if you are asking me which team falls out of the playoffs, they are at the top of the list.”
On the court, the guard room is extremely crowded, which will force general manager Joe Cronin to make decisions sooner rather than later. The move to buy low on Ja Morant could define Portland’s season, although he was acquired for the low cost of salary filler. A fresh start could do wonders for Morant, but he steps into a backcourt alongside Jrue Holiday, Scoot Henderson and Damian Lillard, who will return this season after rehabbing a torn Achilles.
- Anonymous scouts break down each Western Conference team: Clippers | Grizzlies | Jazz | Kings | Lakers | Mavericks | Nuggets | Pelicans | Rockets | Spurs | Suns | Thunder | Timberwolves | Trail Blazers | Warriors
Morant has played 79 total games over the past three seasons as he’s dealt with injuries and a number of off-court issues that led to a messy breakup with the Grizzlies. When available, he’s an electric finisher who can make plays for his teammates, but the issue is Lillard and Avdija also need the ball in their hands. Plus, the Blazers need to figure out if Henderson is a part of their future as he’s headed for restricted free agency next summer.
“We will probably see a more available Ja. He might play in games,” the scout told SI. “He's got a bad knee, doesn't really work on his physical fitness, I doubt that he's all of a sudden become an elite-level shooter, and he's small. So you have that, you've got a bad defender who's a small guard who can't shoot, who physically is unfit, paired next to a small guard who's a bad defender and who can shoot [in Lillard]. So probably going to be tough.”
On the bright side, Avdija is currently on one of the best contracts in the NBA. However, he’s eligible for a contract extension and will be due for a massive payday should his play continue. That wrinkle should keep a heavy load of on-ball work for Avdija, which makes the slew of guards even more questionable. Sharpe will miss considerable time with a torn meniscus, which gives Nori additional minutes to work with as he figures out which backcourt combinations work best. Losing Sharpe is a big loss, but by the time he’s healthy, maybe Portland will have figured out the guard conundrum—possibly through a trade to consolidate the backcourt depth into a much-needed wings.
The issue? Holiday and Morant’s contracts would be incredibly difficult to get off of.
- NBA Championship Power Rankings: Where Does Your Favorite Team Stack Up?
Down low, Donovan Clingan was one of the NBA’s best rebounders last year in just his second season. He’s an elite rim protector, too, but he still has some work to do to prove he’s worthy of a considerable rookie extension, which he’s eligible for next summer.
“Defensively, [the Blazers] need a DPOY type of year from Clingan,” the scout said. “I think he has some upside and can be pretty impactful. Still got to improve his fitness level, but I thought he showed growth from year one to year two, and he continues on that he's probably going to be a nice player. But he is going to have a lot of work to do defending against dribble penetration.”
A promising young center, an All-Star scoring wing and an interesting mix of guards isn’t an awful recipe, but the Blazers will need time to figure out the glaring logjam. Even more important, what version of Morant will Portland get? If the experiment crashes and burns, the Blazers will have his massive salary ($42 million and $44 million) on their books for two more seasons.
It just doesn’t seem like the Blazers have enough to keep up with the Western Conference powers or even the up-and-coming teams like the Jazz.
Offseason Recap
- Who’s in: Ja Morant, Branden Carlson, Jeremy Sochan, Micah Potter, Robert Williams III (re-signed)
- Who’s out: Jerami Grant, Kris Murray, Matisse Thybulle
Roster wise, the only considerable move the Blazers made over the offseason was the splashy trade for Morant. Since his value deteriorated in Memphis, Portland only had to give up Jerami Grant and Kris Murray (and no draft capital) to get the deal done. What the offseason did leave, though, is a lack of depth at forward. After Camara and Avdija, Portland doesn’t have any more true wings unless Jeremy Sochan makes the roster off his training camp deal. And that leaves much to be desired.
Maybe the Blazers trade Henderson for some help, but moving on from the No. 3 pick from three years ago for fill-in depth wouldn’t be great business. Camara certainly helps as a strong perimeter defender, but he can’t do it all by himself aside a lackluster defensive guard duo in Morant and Lillard. Holiday can help offset the defensive concerns, but he’s not getting any younger.
SI’s prediction for the 2026-27 Trail Blazers
The West will be a gauntlet—one the Blazers have too many questions to seriously compete in. Portland will likely hover around the play-in range once again, but the best case in that scenario is a likely series with the Thunder or the Spurs. And we saw how that worked out for the Blazers last year. More importantly, Portland’s year is about picking a direction moving forward.

Blake Silverman is a writer at Sports Illustrated, primarily covering the NBA and WNBA. Before joining SI in November 2024 as a breaking/trending news writer, he covered the WNBA, NBA, G League and college basketball for numerous sites, including Winsidr, SB Nation and A10Talk. He’s an alum of both Michigan State and St. Bonaventure University, receiving a master’s degree from the Bonnies’ sports journalism program. Outside of work, he’s a husband, father, yogi and fairly mediocre tennis player who’s open to any tips on how to play defense in EA Sports College Football.

item.content:encoded:
It might sound like hyperbole, but the fallout from losing Jaxson Dart has a franchise-altering trickle-down effect on the New York Giants. Everyone is impacted by his suddenly bleak 2026 outlook, so why not start at the top with general manager Joe Schoen?
The Giants signed Schoen to a multi-year deal back in May, suggesting his job is safe — for now. But as former Baltimore Ravens head coach Brian Billick said, based on his own experience: "Signing a big contract extension doesn't mean you're going to be there, necessarily; it just means you're going to be paid."
For better or worse, the NFL is a results-driven business, and Schoen's track record precedes him in the worst way. New York is tied for the third-fewest wins in the league since he was hired in 2022 (23) and has posted three straight losing campaigns. His leash has been stretched surprisingly far, and expectations were raised with John Harbaugh's arrival, making Dart's availability (or lack thereof) a potential death knell.
How does Jaxson Dart's gutting injury affect Giants GM Joe Schoen?
Things have quickly gone from bad to worse to possibly catastrophic. Dart tried to reenter the game after getting hurt in the Giants' disastrous 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. He was eventually ruled out for the night with what was initially believed to be an MCL sprain, which has devolved into a doomsday scenario.
If their showing against the Rams is any indication, New York is in trouble without Dart. The offense cratered following his departure from the contest, and the defense doesn't appear ready to pick up the slack. Put it all together, and Big Blue could be headed toward another lost season under Schoen.
Maneuvering for Dart (and star wide receiver Malik Nabers) has arguably been Schoen's biggest achievement with the G-Men. It's not easy to identify a game-changing talent at football's most important position. However, the football gods can taketh as easily as they giveth.
Does John Harbaugh lose patience?
Lest we forget, Schoen found himself on the losing end of a reported "power struggle" this offseason. He ceded the high ground in the Giants' new hierarchy centered around Harbaugh. In other words, the only reason the former wasn't only retained but also extended is that the latter OK'd the move.
Situations like this are fluid, though, and don't account for the absence of the club's most valuable player. The duo has gone on the record to let us all know that their working relationship is a collaborative effort and they're in sync. One wrong turn, especially involving Dart, may prompt Harbaugh to make changes, with moving on from Schoen being the easiest adjustment for the front office.
New York sinking sans Dart would be a massive indictment of the roster Schoen's had a hand in putting together. Of course, this squad has several Harbaugh recruits from his Baltimore days, yet there are 100 million reasons why he won't be the fall guy.

item.content:encoded:
It just shows you the urgency of Steelers week at Paycor Stadium.
As Al Golden walked off the Reliant Stadium field Sunday with the biggest prize of his 19 games as the Bengals defensive coordinator, he looked like he was headed to a root canal instead of a locker room celebration.
The 2-0 Bengals head to Pittsburgh Sunday (1 p.m.-Cincinnati's Local 12), where the Steelers have amassed the only home winning percentage above 70% in the 57 seasons of the AFL-NFL merger.
"I was on to Pittsburgh. I know it's unfortunate. I mean, I was onto it. I was gone already," Golden told the media the Monday after his men hadn't allowed a touchdown in Houston.
Golden probably won't be soothed by Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow's 3-1 record in Pittsburgh and that he's won his last three starts at the Three Rivers. Instead, Golden is wondering, "What are they seeing? What we just saw? What are they seeing that fits with what they do and what are we going to see again? What do we need to stop?"
Golden even dropped his go-to quote from The Godfather.
"I know a lot of people want to stop and celebrate, but that's not the world that we've chosen," Golden said. "I say it all the time. Hyman Roth. This is the business we've chosen, and you've got to move on. And this league does not wait for anybody.
"This is the AFC North, this is the Pittsburgh Steelers in Pittsburgh, Aaron Rodgers, Mike McCarthy, we're moving on."
Short Yardage Goes Long Way
Golden may have a short memory, but he has great recall when it comes to Sunday's two biggest plays. Both coming on short yardage. Defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence II blew up a fourth-and-one at the Bengals 18 in a scoreless second quarter, and in the third quarter tackle T.J. Slaton stuffed a third-and-one that forced a short 58-yard field-goal try with the Bengals clinging to a 10-3 lead.
But Golden also saw a busy Demetrius Knight Jr., the linebacker who backed up both stops, as well as edge Cedric Johnson, safety Jordan Battle, and cornerback Dax Hill.
"Obviously, Dex did an awesome job on the first one. I think Ced Johnson setting the edge there on the first one, Jordan Battle fitting the C gap on the first one, and then (Knight) coming from the backside, that was really good.
"On the second one, it was a little bit of a different look and T.J. played into the tackle really well. Dax was on that side now as a corner and fit it really nice and we set the edge on that one as well."
Just Enough Ced
Speaking of Cedric Johnson, the third-year defensive end from Ole Miss, has four sacks in his last three games dating back to last season after Sunday's two. A sixth-round pick, Johnson was inactive for seven games as a rookie in 2024 and missed the first eight games last year with a calf injury.
But ever since he came back in a reserve role, all he does is produce. He recovered his first two career fumbles in the Thanksgiving Night win in Baltimore and hasn't stopped. He played 22 snaps that night and worked 23 Sunday in Houston after playing 19 in the opener. That was the second fewest in Sunday's line rotation. Only edge Shemar Stewart had fewer snaps (five) and he had a sack, too, as defensive line coach Jerry Montgomery went for the economy pack.
"You do (feel the rotation) because you just look at Shemar's sack. Shemar's fresh in the game, chipping the back and sees a gap and is able to explode through there because he's fresh," said head coach Zac Taylor Monday. "You're able to put fresh guys in the game at that moment. That's just so critical to be able to have that depth, keep those guys fresh over the course of the game, and not put too many snaps on them.
"And you're not taking them out because you feel like they need a breather, but you're worried about who's going in. We don't really have that concern now. Everybody's playing at a high level, and so we just got to keep that up."
Taylor, by the way, not only loves what Johnson has been giving them, but how.
"Ced's an easy guy to pull for because he just kind of goes about his business and is dependable and you've got to have those types of guys on your 53 and Ced has been one of those guys for us," Taylor said. "He's a really dependable player for us, and somebody we can count on. I thought he did a really good job in the run game last week against Tampa. This week he got to pay off in the pass game as well."
Cashing In On Cashius
Golden is still amazed the Bengals were able to draft Texas A&M edge Cashius Howell in the second round at No. 41 and rolled him out for 41 snaps, more than half the 80 plays. According to Pro Football Focus, Howell had seven pressures in a game the web site ticketed the Bengals for 44 with an astounding 54.5% win rate.
When Johnson racked up the last "coffin nails," sack, it was Howell, just missing his first NFL sack, who set him up with a clean shot off the edge against left tackle Aireontae Ersery as part of a three-man rush. Howell also battled with 380-pound right tackle Trent Brown, despite a weight difference of about 130 pounds or so.
"No, he didn't," said Howell, when asked if Golden gave him a number of pressures. "But I'll take one if you got it."
Told it was about five pressures and maybe more, Howell thought and said, "Let's do that for at least 15 more weeks."
"As a rusher, he knows exactly who he is. He's got a speed, he's got a dip, he's got to counter off that," Golden said. "That's three, that's all he needs. He plays with a high motor. I thought he set the edge really well for us (Sunday), especially as big as Trenton is. And then he gives you two, three drops a game, which is awesome. It just makes us so much more versatile. And he's doing all those things for us right now, which is great."
Howell said last Friday that he needed to improve his quickness off the snap.
"Nothing specific, but just being intentional about it over the course of the week at practice," Howell said. "Keep loading up that front foot and just getting off the ball."
Slants and Screens
Asked what Burrow's practice status is this week after going full only once last week with a tight back, Taylor offered, "I think I know the answer to that, but I don't want to give you that right now." …
Knight tied his career-high with 12 tackles and got a game ball. His traveling leather cowboy hat was a perfect match, but he didn't buy it just for the Houston trip. "I'm a hat guy," Knight said. "I bought it first thing in the offseason."
He also wore cowboy boots on the way in, but he carried them back home: "Not after playing a three-hour football game." …
Knight's 19 tackles are seven away from Titans linebacker Anthony Hill's NFL-leading 26 …
Everything went right for the Bengals' special teams Sunday. Kicker Evan McPherson perfect from beyond 50 yards. Four Ryan Rehkow punts inside the 20. Seven Texans drive starts inside the 25.
And they camethisclose to an opening kick return touchdown by wide receiver Dohnte Meyers. Meyers looked like he was headed there in his second NFL game when he stumbled after his career-long 40-yarder.
"I saw a lot of daylight. I know that. It was perfectly blocked. I just followed the way it was drawn up," Meyers said. "I think my eyes and my mind saw it before my feet did. That was not a good combination." …
Meyers is showing why they tapped him to replace Charlie Jones as the primary returner. He's shown soft hands catching punts and has displayed a knack for coming up and making catches before they bounce.
"I think I was too deep on a couple, but I'm comfortable back there," Meyers said …

item.content:encoded:
Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty!, 2026.
Directed by Josef Kubota Wladyka.
Starring Rinko Kikuchi, Alberto Guerra, Alejandro Edda, You, Yoh Yoshida, Charley Flyte, Soji Arai, Chelsea Gonzalez, Derek Mio, and Damián Alcázar.
SYNOPSIS:
Haru and Luis love competing in Tokyo’s ballroom dance scene, but after tragedy strikes, Haru withdraws into isolation. When friends coax her back to the studio, she develops an infatuation with the new instructor.
Everything from an exploration of the powerful connectivity of music and dance transcending language (there is a combination of Japanese, Spanish, and English here all distinctly colored and stylized for clarity), open relationships, and a fantastical study of grief, co-writer/director Josef Kubota Wladyka (penning the screenplay alongside Nicholas Huynh, the movie is dedicated to the filmmaker’s dancer mother) Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! is a strange film that will work one moment and possibly feel a bit too whimsical or odd the next.
With a slightly overlong opening, the filmmakers introduce viewers to the lives of Haru (Rinko Kikuchi) and Luis (Alejandro Edda), a rumba-dancing married couple living a quiet, happy life before the latter has a heart attack during their routine lessons. Even nine months removed from Luis’ death, Haru is living in isolation and won’t even come out of the house to celebrate her birthday. She has also started hallucinating seeing Luis at night inside of a black bird costume, no doubt symbolizing the grief she can’t move on from.
Eventually, her friends have had enough of this and basically force her out of the house (one is dialed back, the other is horny and obsessed with sleeping around through dating apps) to take up more dancing lessons, where the three of them come into the sphere of instructor Fedir (Alberto Guerra), absurdly attractive and accomplished but also married. However, after some digging by Haru’s relatives, they learn that he is in an open marriage, which prompts her to research this dynamic, which appears to be unheard of in Japanese culture. Understandably, Haru seems to think all of this is crazy, but she also appears to view Fedir as a potential replacement for her lost love.
In secret, away from her friends, Haru makes her move on Fedir, which allows the film to enter its magical musical groove, complete with imaginative sequences, such as one in which a fight against some street hoodlums harassing the woman transitions into a blend of punches and dance choreography. Another winning moment sees Haru take Fedir to a Japanese dance show, where Fedir is unsure whether he will understand what is happening. That is, until everything breaks out into numbers set to music from Dirty Dancing (if it wasn’t obvious by now, the soundtrack here is wonderful, with Japanese arrangements of well-known Western songs).
From the bright color palette to the costume to the choreography itself, those segments are what give the film most of its charm. In trying to function as a lighthearted take on grief and reinvigoration through life and art, there are also some interesting points made about love and the reactions of those who are in love with someone else. There are reservations to be had about where the open marriage aspect ultimately goes, but Ha-Chan, Shake Your Booty! remains an idiosyncratic, intentionally messy (just like life), and uplifting look at moving on. The dramatic beats don’t always click, but it is vibrantly acted with equally rising musical numbers and undeniable inventiveness at the helm in director Josef Kubota Wladyka.
Flickering Myth Rating – Film: ★ ★ ★ / Movie: ★ ★ ★
Robert Kojder

Tom Parker’s widow Kelsey Parker found a second chance at love with boyfriend Will Lindsay while coping with grief.
Kelsey and Tom were married from 2018 until his death in March 2022 at age 33. The Wanted member died following his battle with brain cancer. Kelsey and Tom welcomed two children, Aurelia and Bodhi, in July 2019 and October 2020, respectively.
Years after Tom’s passing, Kelsey shared that she was dating again and revealed her new romance with Lindsay in September 2024. Four months later, Kelsey announced that she was pregnant with her and Lindsay’s first child.
“Tom and I always said we wanted four — but life had other plans,” she told The Mirror in January 2025. “So yes, this is amazing but also bittersweet. The joys of finding out I’m pregnant and moving forward with my life, while thinking, ‘My life could have been so different. I’ve felt every emotion under the sun.”
In June 2025, Kelsey announced the loss of their baby, sharing that he was “born sleeping.”
“Phoenix Parker-Lindsay, you will forever be loved,” she wrote via Instagram at the time.
Keep scrolling for a complete timeline of Kelsey and Lindsay’s relationship:
September 2024
Two years after Tom’s death, Kelsey made her Lindsay’s romance Instagram Official. The post included a photo of the couple hugging while Lindsay’s head turned away from the camera and was captioned with a single red heart emoji. After making their relationship official, Kelsey took to social media to thank fans for their kind words.
“I was really hesitant to share this part of my life, especially since many of you know me from my life with Tom and the horrific grief I’ve been dealing with after losing him,” she penned. “Opening up about my journey over the past couple of years has been incredibly healing, allowing me to connect with others who’ve gone through similar experiences and build a beautiful, supportive community.”
October 2024
During an October 2024 episode of Kelsey’s “Mum’s the Word” podcast with Georgia Jones, Kelsey shared that she and Lindsay “met authentically” and they had already introduced each other to their families.
“He just makes me really happy. And I think for me, I’ve been trying to find happiness for a little while now. I’m always going to have that guilt, I guess that’s part of the grief process.” she explained. “Having the guilt that I’m here and I’ve met someone but it will never take away the love I had for Tom. And with Will he would never try and take that away from me either.”
November 2024
While appearing on the British talk show Lorraine, Kelsey gave some more details about how she and Lindsay first connected.
“We met out with friends, he was out with a group of boys and I was out with a group of girls and we just had a connection,” she gushed. “I just wanted to meet someone authentic. I couldn’t have done [a] dating app, I was so scared and it was the judgment from people about moving on and meeting someone, but everyone’s so supportive.”
January 2025
Kelsey and Lindsay announced that they were expecting their first child together.
“I’m over the moon. This is something I’ve wanted for a long time,” Lindsay told The Mirror. “I couldn’t be happier and I know Kelsey is going to be an amazing mum, as she already is.”
April 2025
Lindsay and Kelsey took a family trip to Gran Canaria, Spain.
“Nothing beats a family holiday to Gran Canaria!!” Kelsey wrote via Instagram alongside a photo of the family of the group out to dinner. “These trips will always have a special place in our hearts, we always have the best time ☀️ Soaking up these moments before our family grows… 🤰🏼.”
June 2025
Kelsey announced that she and Lindsay lost their baby, whom they named Phoenix. The post included a poem written in honor of the late newborn, who was born stillborn.
“For Phoenix, Born Sleeping, Forever Loved,” the poem began. “The world grew quiet as you arrived / So loved, so longed for, yet not alive / Our precious boy, our angel light / Born with wings, took silent flight. We named you Phoenix, brave and bright / A soul of love, of warmth and light / Though we never heard you cry / You’ll live in hearts that won’t ask why. No breath you drew, no eyes to see / Still, you mean everything to me / You’ll journey with us, softly near / In every sigh, in every tear.”
May 2026
Kelsey announced her pregnancy with her and Lindsay’s rainbow baby nearly one year after Phoenix’s death.
“A year ago next month, we lost our beautiful baby boy, Phoenix 🤍,” she wrote via Instagram. “And somehow, through all the heartbreak, it feels like Tom and Phoenix have sent us another little gift from heaven our little rainbow baby ✨.”
September 2026
Kelsey and Lindsay welcomed daughter River, calling her “our little bit of hope.”

item.content:encoded:
Pedro Acosta is finally a MotoGP race winner, after he took an emotional first victory at the Austrian Grand Prix on KTM’s home turf.
The Spaniard had to wait 56 premier class starts before he could break his duck, something that seemed unfathomable when he made his debut at the start of the 2024 season.
Acosta was quick from the off at the Red Bull Ring, but he had to win the grand prix the hard way on Sunday.
A certain victory in the sprint was thrown away when he crashed with three laps to go, while he left his KTM team with more repair work to do on Sunday morning when he fell in warm-up.
But once he took the lead on lap nine of 28 in the main race, he never looked back, as he had the measure of Aprilia’s Jorge Martin.
It’s a win that closes a circle for the Acosta/KTM relationship, with the 22-year-old moving on to Ducati next season.
But could it get even better for both parties in the remaining races of 2026?
Though 72 points adrift in the standings, Marc Marquez firmly considers Acosta a title contender and has already branded him the favourite for the upcoming Japanese Grand Prix.
On the latest Crash MotoGP Podcast, Amy Reynolds is joined by Lewis Duncan and Peter McLaren to discuss the Austrian Grand Prix and whether or not Acosta can still fight for the 2026 title.
The team also discuss Acosta’s character and what to expect long-term when he goes up against Marc Marquez at Ducati in 2027.
Elsewhere, they discuss Jorge Martin’s strong weekend and his 12-point lead in the championship, asking if this is the Spaniard’s true return to form.
Ducati’s difficult weekend at the Red Bull Ring is analysed, as most of its riders were well off the pace, while Marc Marquez battled a brake issue in the grand prix.

Some of the best romance movies ever made have tackled some difficult territory, examining the complicated topics of marriage and divorce alike. While many of the most satisfying endings seen in film have closed happily, some of the strongest dramatic entries have taken a harder look at emotions, chronicling the difficult dissolutions of relationships and marriages.
Movies about divorces are not always easy to watch. Many such stories delve into the complex emotional turmoil that the falling apart of a relationship can hold. Loaded with heartbreak and genuine pain, these stories provide deep points of connection that can help anyone going through such a struggle find ways to still feel human.
However, considering a marriage that ends in divorce to be a failure is such a limiting way of looking at the world.
Seeing the connections that blossom between two people, even if they do not last forever, is an important emotional factor in movies about humans and relationships. Not every love lasts forever, but this does not take away from the value that it has provided to a life.
Sometimes letting go of a relationship is worth celebrating, not just grieving. Many of these complex films examine the fallouts of those relationships in different and often surprising ways. Moving on is a part of life, and seeing how that works can fill these stories with sadness, joy, humor, and heartbreak all at once, making these films essential watches.
Divorce Italian Style
An unusual look at marriage and divorce, this fantastic 1961 comedy directed by Pietro Germi deeply questions a number of confusing social mores. In the film, Ferdinando, a poor Sicilian nobleman played by Marcello Mastroianni, falls in love with his sixteen-year-old cousin, Angela, and wishes to be with her.
However, Ferdinando is married, and divorce is illegal. However, considering the law's lax treatment of honor killings, he devises an absurd path to being with Angela: he will secretly find his wife a new lover, catch them in the act, and murder her. After serving a short prison sentence, he will be able to be with Angela.
This convoluted path highlights major issues with Italian law, and does so with great humor. A twisted and hilarious story, Divorce Italian Style is one of the more outsized and comedic looks at marriage and relationships on this list.
War Of The Roses
Danny DeVito has directed some fantastic films, and War of the Roses might be his best. This dark and funny 1989 comedy examines the dissolution of a marriage between Oliver and Barbara Rose, played by Michael Douglas and Kathleen Turner respectively. Rounding out the cast, DeVito plays their lawyer.
While the marriage between the Roses at first seems idyllic, cracks appear quickly and constantly throughout the film's runtime. The story turns into an unsettling war of a divorce that, while often hilarious, is also palpable in its cruelty, making the film a challenge for some to watch.
Still, based on a novel by Warren Adler, The War of the Roses is full of great substance, and is an entertaining, even if sometimes difficult, watch. The story was also recently remade in another strong film, 2025's The Roses.
A Separation
Global cinema has given excellent insight into how marriages and divorces function throughout the world, and A Separation is one of the strongest examples of this. Asghar Farhadi's 2011 Iranian drama was a huge achievement, and even won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
Built around family complications, the film sees Simin looking to leave Iran with their daughter in order to find a better life. Meanwhile, her husband wishes to stay, due to his father's medical needs. The film escalates, examining the complexities of family duties, immigration, and Iran's legal system.
A thoughtful film with a great deal to say, A Separation gives a fantastic look at relationships in Iran, and how even the most well-meaning characters can have their intentions corrupted by the machinations of separation.
Possession (1981)
The 1981 horror film Possession, which is itself being remade for 2027, is a fantastic entry in the genre. Sam Neill plays Mark, a spy who returns home only to learn that his wife, Anna, is sleeping with someone else and wishes to file for divorce.
The film leans into the texture of its Cold War setting, and highlights great feelings of alienation.
As a horror film, Possession goes to some interesting places. Director Andrzej Żuławski uses supernatural horrors in the film to express the psychological destruction of a relationship falling apart, as Mark discovers a terrifying creature with some shocking implications for the film's story.
Terrifying and raw all at once, the human story behind Possession is what makes it so strong. A horror with fantastic depth, it is an essential genre watch in the canon of films about divorce.
Kramer Vs. Kramer
Movies about heartbreak are necessarily difficult, but they can also show growth in unexpected ways. The 1979 legal drama Kramer vs. Kramer is a fantastic example of this, built around the separation and eventual divorce of Ted and Joanna Kramer, played by Dustin Hoffman and Meryl Streep, respectively.
The film took an unprecedented look at gender roles, uniquely examining a father's place in caring for his child. When Joanna suddenly decides to leave her marriage, it is up to Ted to stay behind and commit himself to his relationship with his son, giving the child a loving home throughout devastating emotional turmoil.
Giving eyes into a contentious battle for custody, the film shows the ruthlessness that a divorce can bring out between two people who love one another. However, its focus on family helps to make Kramer vs. Kramer one of the best movies of the 1970s.
Stepmom
While not a perfect movie, there is much to enjoy in the 1998 film Stepmom. The film takes a complex eye to changing ideas of what makes up a family, telling the story of two women navigating their place in looking after a pair of children.
Susan Sarandon plays Jackie Harrison, a divorced mother who has been diagnosed with a terminal illness. To complicate her life further, as she attempts to co-parent her two children along with her ex-husband, Luke's new girlfriend, Julia Roberts' Isabel, moves in and creates a whole new dynamic within the family.
Balancing ideas about parenting and caretaking, the film takes some surprisingly thoughtful turns, even if it occasionally leans a little saccharine. With great performances at its core, it remains an excellent film.
Is This Thing On?
An unusually interesting look at processing the dissolution of a relationship, Bradley Cooper's Is This Thing On? centers on the dynamics between Will Arnett's Alex and Laura Dern's Tess. Married long ago, and now in their forties, each reckons with the fact that they have given up things for their dynamic and to raise children together.
Their split is not bitter, and the two move on to a new phase in each of their lives. Tess dedicates herself to coaching, while Alex turns to the world of stand-up comedy, which helps to process how he really feels about his life and his relationships.
A complex look at marriage and divorce, Is This Thing On? brings a unique lens to a complicated subject, and creates something that feels both honest and genuinely thoughtful.
Crazy, Stupid, Love
Crazy, Stupid, Love is a compelling and smart romantic comedy that is full of fantastic stars. Steve Carell plays the central role of Cal, a middle-aged man whose wife asks him for a divorce. Unprepared for these events, he is helped by Jacob, an attractive and charismatic younger man played by Ryan Gosling, to meet women.
Of course, things quickly get messy. Jacob meets and falls in love with Emma Stone's Hannah, who turns out to be Cal's daughter. The dynamics become confused, and real questions about relationships, lifestyles, and suitability for partnership come to the fore.
Crazy, Stupid, Love confronts some real concerns about attraction, relationships, and showing up for one another. The script is genuinely funny and charming, and the characters are excellent.
Mrs. Doubtfire
One of the strongest movies that defined Robin Williams' career, Mrs. Doubtfire is a fantastic comedy that hinges on a stunningly charismatic performance. The film centers around Daniel Hillard, who, after his wife files for divorce, finds himself losing custody of his children until he is able to find and maintain a steady job.
In response, Daniel launches a scheme that is silly, but full of heart. He disguises himself as Euphegenia Doubtfire and takes on a job in his family home as a nanny. This affords him the opportunity to maintain a relationship with his children while also working a second job at a TV station.
The premise is a bit outsized and silly, but the execution is what makes the movie so strong. Williams balances comedy and real emotion as both Daniel and Mrs. Doubtfire, allowing the heavy subject matter of the film to be even more effective.
The Awful Truth (1937)
A silly, screwball comedy from the 1930s, The Awful Truth is an amusing story about a couple who enter into proceedings for divorce. There is a 90-day waiting period to process it, and in the meantime, each of the two pursues other romantic connections.
Still, neither seems to be able to let go of the other, and is unwilling to see them with anyone else. Cary Grant's Jerry and Irene Dunne's Lucy sabotage each other's new relationships at every turn, resulting in some excellent humor.
The stars had great chemistry, and the film relied heavily on their shared charisma as well as improvisation. It remains one of the best romantic comedies in the history of classic Hollywood.
